title: Local diamond for two exceptional rational-component contractions
statement: Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure], let $(P,M)$ be a semistable multipointed $k$-curve [def-trf-multipointed-curve, def-trf-multipointed-curve-modification], and let $r:P\to C$ be a proper morphism [def-weil-proper-morphism] of $k$-schemes [def-pc-scheme] (a $k$-morphism). Assume that the image under $r$ of every connected component [def-weil-connected-scheme] of $P$ contains more than one point. Call an irreducible component $A\simeq\mathbf P^1_k$ [def-sc-p1-standard] exceptional when $r(A)$ is a singleton and $A$ contains at most two distinct points of $M\cup P_{\mathrm{sing}}$, where $P_{\mathrm{sing}}$ is the nonsmooth locus. An elementary contraction of $A$ is a scheme pushout [def-weil-pbc-category-colimit] of $P\leftarrow A\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum] whose quotient pair $(P_A,M_A)$ is semistable, whose marking map $M\to M_A$ is an isomorphism, and through which $r$ factors. For every supplied elementary contraction $h_A:P\to P_A$, its curve map is proper [def-weil-proper-morphism] and surjective with connected geometric fibres [def-weil-geometric-fibre], is an isomorphism $P\setminus A\simeq P_A\setminus\{h_A(A)\}$, and its induced reference map $r_A:P_A\to C$ is proper and again has image containing more than one point on every connected component. If $A\ne B$ are exceptional components and elementary contractions $h_A:P\to P_A$ and $h_B:P\to P_B$ are supplied, then $h_A|_B$ and $h_B|_A$ identify $B$ and $A$ with exceptional irreducible components $B_A\subset P_A$ and $A_B\subset P_B$ for the induced reference maps. There exist elementary contractions $j_A:(P_A,M_A)\to(T,N)$ of $B_A$ and $j_B:(P_B,M_B)\to(T,N)$ of $A_B$ to the same semistable multipointed curve, with compatible reference map to $C$, such that $j_Ah_A=j_Bh_B$ as morphisms of pointed $k$-curves. No connectedness, separatedness or properness of the structural maps to $k$ is assumed.

source.place: Appendix B, printed p. 58, elementary exceptional-component pushouts preceding Lemma B.3 and the exceptional-tree argument in its proof. The relative noncollapse hypothesis excludes the absolute unstable cases mentioned after B.3; local diamond formulation and induction are supplied by the worker. Primary PDF read online; archival copy WANTED.

proof.text: Fix one exceptional component $A$. The semistable curve is reduced by [lem-trf-nodal-geometric-fibres-reduced]. Put $Q=\overline{P\setminus A}_{\mathrm{red}}$. By [lem-trf-nodal-subcurve-boundary] applied to the subcurve $A$, whose complementary closure is $Q$, $E=A\cap Q$ is a finite reduced set of nodes of $P$, smooth on both $A$ and $Q$. Applied instead to the subcurve $Q$, whose complementary closure is $A$ (as $P\setminus Q\subseteq A$ is a nonempty open of the irreducible $A$), the same lemma shows that $Q$ is nodal; $Q$ is of finite type and pure of dimension one over $k$, so $(Q,\varnothing)$ is a semistable multipointed $k$-curve. Since $A$ itself is smooth, every singular point of $P$ on $A$ lies in $E$: a node not meeting $Q$ would be a singular point of $A$. If $E$ were empty, $A$ would be an open-and-closed connected component of $P$, contrary to noncollapse. Thus $d=|E|\in\{1,2\}$. If $m=|M\cap A|$, the disjointness of markings and nodes gives $m+d\le2$. The reduced subcurves $A,Q$ have scheme-theoretic union $P$: their two ideals intersect to zero since $P$ is reduced and their supports cover $P$. Therefore [lem-trf-closed-union-pushout] gives $P=Q\amalg_E A$. Finally $Q\to C$ is proper by [lem-weil-pbc-closed-immersion-proper].

source.place: Appendix B, printed p. 58: elementary exceptional-component contraction paragraph preceding Lemma B.3; local diamond argument supplied here. Primary source read at https://arxiv.org/pdf/0707.3953, PDF page 58; archival copy WANTED.

proof.text: The singleton-image map $A\to C$ factors through a $k$-point $c:\operatorname{Spec}k\to C$. Indeed choose an affine neighbourhood of its image. Global regular functions on $A\simeq\mathbf P^1_k$ are $k$: on the standard two charts of [def-sc-p1-standard] a section is a polynomial in $t$ and also a polynomial in $t^{-1}$, hence constant. Thus the affine-target morphism is induced by a ring map into $k$, a $k$-algebra map because $r$ is a $k$-morphism. Apply [lem-trf-relative-nodal-point-pinching] to the proper $k$-morphism $Q\to C$ and $E\to\operatorname{Spec}k$, over $c$, to obtain $Y=Q\amalg_E\operatorname{Spec}k$ proper over $C$, with finite map $v:Q\to Y$. The union pushout of Step 1 gives $h:P\to Y$. For any target, a map out of $Y$ is exactly a map from $Q$ and a map from $\operatorname{Spec}k$ agreeing on $E$; equivalently it is a map from $P$ whose restriction to $A$ is that constant map. Consequently $Y$ is the pushout of $P\leftarrow A\to\operatorname{Spec}k$. Any supplied elementary contraction is uniquely isomorphic to this one, with its point leg and factorization to $C$.

source.place: Appendix B, printed p. 58: elementary exceptional-component contraction paragraph preceding Lemma B.3; local diamond argument supplied here. Primary source read at https://arxiv.org/pdf/0707.3953, PDF page 58; archival copy WANTED.

proof.text: Write $y=h(A)$. Away from $y$ the pinching theorem gives $P\setminus A\simeq Y\setminus\{y\}$. The fibre over $y$ is $A$ scheme-theoretically: away from $E$ this is immediate, while at each point of $E$ the completed nodal ring of $P$ is $k[[x,z]]/(xz)$ with $A$ cut out by $x$; the pinching description sends the maximal ideal at $y$ to $(x)$. Thus every geometric fibre is a point or $\mathbf P^1$, and is connected; the map is surjective. It is proper by [lem-weil-pbc-proper-to-separated], since $P\to C$ is proper and $Y\to C$ is proper, hence separated. If $d=1$, $y$ is smooth and $m\le1$; move the possible unique marking on $A$ to $y$. If $d=2$, $y$ is a node and $m=0$. All other markings are unchanged. They remain distinct smooth closed points, so this gives a semistable marking $M_Y$ with $M\simeq M_Y$. This constructs an elementary contraction even when one was not supplied.

source.place: Appendix B, printed p. 58: elementary exceptional-component contraction paragraph preceding Lemma B.3; local diamond argument supplied here. Primary source read at https://arxiv.org/pdf/0707.3953, PDF page 58; archival copy WANTED.

proof.text: Noncollapse is preserved by every such contraction. The finitely many connected components $P_i$ of $P$ are open and closed. Their images under the proper surjection $h$ are closed, connected, cover $Y$, and are pairwise disjoint: a fibre meeting two $P_i$ would be disconnected. Finiteness makes these images open as well, so they are precisely the connected components of $Y$. For each one, $r_Y(h(P_i))=r(P_i)$ has more than one point. In addition $r_Y$ is proper by the pinching theorem. This proves all permanence assertions and supplies exactly the hypotheses needed to repeat Steps 1--3 on the quotient.

source.place: Appendix B, printed p. 58: elementary exceptional-component contraction paragraph preceding Lemma B.3; local diamond argument supplied here. Primary source read at https://arxiv.org/pdf/0707.3953, PDF page 58; archival copy WANTED.

proof.text: Now let $A\ne B$ be exceptional. Their intersection is a reduced set of nodes by the boundary statement, and contains at most two points. If it contained two, these exhaust all singular points on each of $A,B$, so no third component could meet $A\cup B$. Their union would be an open-and-closed connected component, and the two singleton reference images agree at their intersection. This contradicts noncollapse. Hence $|A\cap B|\le1$. In the pinching construction for $A$, the component $B\subset Q$ meets the unique pinched fibre $E$ in at most one point. The subcurve clause of [lem-trf-relative-nodal-point-pinching] shows that $h_A|_B$ is a closed immersion and identifies $B$ with its reduced image $B_A$. This image is an irreducible component: $Q\to P_A$ is finite and an isomorphism away from finitely many closed points, so the generic points, and their closures, correspond. In particular $B_A\simeq\mathbf P^1_k$, with singleton reference image.

source.place: Appendix B, printed p. 58: elementary exceptional-component contraction paragraph preceding Lemma B.3; local diamond argument supplied here. Primary source read at https://arxiv.org/pdf/0707.3953, PDF page 58; archival copy WANTED.

proof.text: Check the special points on $B_A$. If $A\cap B=\varnothing$, the contraction point lies off $B_A$ and nothing changes on $B$. Otherwise write $e=A\cap B$. For $d=1$, the old node $e$ becomes smooth, unmarked if $m=0$ and marked if $m=1$. For $d=2$, the second point of $E$ is not on $B$, by Step 5; $e$ is replaced by the new node $y$, and there is no marking on $A$. In each case the number of distinct special points on $B_A$ is no larger than on $B$. Thus $B_A$ is exceptional. Interchanging $A,B$ proves the identical assertion for $A_B$. By Step 4, $r_A,r_B$ are proper and satisfy noncollapse, so Steps 1--3 applied to these exceptional components produce elementary contractions $j_A:P_A\to T_A$ of $B_A$ and $j_B:P_B\to T_B$, with semistable markings transported isomorphically and induced reference maps to $C$.

source.place: Appendix B, printed p. 58: elementary exceptional-component contraction paragraph preceding Lemma B.3; local diamond argument supplied here. Primary source read at https://arxiv.org/pdf/0707.3953, PDF page 58; archival copy WANTED.

proof.text: The composite $f_A=j_Ah_A$ is constant on both $A$ and $B$. The pushout property of $h_B$ first gives $v:P_B\to T_A$ with $vh_B=f_A$. Since $h_B|_A$ is an isomorphism onto $A_B$, $v$ is constant on $A_B$. The pushout property of $j_B$ then gives $\alpha:T_B\to T_A$ with $\alpha j_Bh_B=j_Ah_A$. The symmetric construction gives $\beta:T_A\to T_B$ with $\beta j_Ah_A=j_Bh_B$. These maps are over $C$ and preserve the transported markings: the reference and marking equations hold after the respective quotient maps, whose universal properties determine the factorizations uniquely.

source.place: Appendix B, printed p. 58: elementary exceptional-component contraction paragraph preceding Lemma B.3; local diamond argument supplied here. Primary source read at https://arxiv.org/pdf/0707.3953, PDF page 58; archival copy WANTED.

proof.text: Each contraction $h$ here is an epimorphism for morphisms of schemes. To check cancellation directly, choose a $k$-point $a:\operatorname{Spec}k\to A$. Its point leg $i:\operatorname{Spec}k\to P_A$ equals $h|_A\,a$. Thus maps agreeing after $h$ also agree after $i$, and uniqueness in the pushout makes them equal. The same applies to $j_A,j_B$, since their contracted components are projective lines. The identities of Step 7 imply $\alpha\beta j_Ah_A=j_Ah_A$ and $\beta\alpha j_Bh_B=j_Bh_B$; cancellation twice gives $\alpha\beta=1$ and $\beta\alpha=1$. Take $(T,N)=(T_A,M_{T_A})$ and replace $j_B$ by $\alpha j_B$. Composition with this isomorphism preserves its pushout property and semistable marking. Then $j_Ah_A=j_Bh_B$ as pointed $k$-morphisms over $C$, as required.
